title: Who has what
hook: The metals in your phone and car, and the food on your plate, come from surprisingly few places.
notes: Mine production and reserves: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026; 2025 values are USGS estimates. Shares are of the USGS world total. US production of some minerals (e.g. lithium) is withheld by USGS and missing here. Gallium is low-purity primary production. Trade: CEPII BACI, version 202601, values in US dollars; the 'lithium ore' group uses HS 253090, a catch-all code that also contains other minerals. Crops: FAOSTAT 2024 (palm oil 2023), including FAO estimates.

scenes.title: Who mines what
scenes.text: Pick a resource. For many of the minerals that batteries, magnets and chips need, one country mines most of the world's supply.

options.label: Lithium
options.text: Lithium goes into batteries. Australia mines about a third of it from hard rock; Chile and Argentina pump it out of salt-flat brines. China (21%) and Zimbabwe (10%) are fast-growing producers.

options.label: Cobalt
options.text: About three-quarters of the world's cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, mostly as a by-product of copper mining in the south. Indonesia, a by-product of its nickel boom, is now second with 14%.

options.label: Rare earths
options.text: Rare earths make the strong magnets in electric motors and wind turbines. China mines about 69% of them; the United States, Australia and Myanmar most of the rest.

options.label: Graphite
options.text: Natural graphite forms the anode of most lithium-ion batteries. China mines about 78% of it.

options.label: Nickel
options.text: Indonesia now mines two-thirds of the world's nickel. It banned exports of raw ore in 2020, which pulled smelters, mostly Chinese-financed, into the country.

options.label: Copper
options.text: Copper carries electricity, so electrification needs ever more of it. Chile (23%), Congo (14%) and Peru (12%) are the largest miners.

options.label: Gallium
options.text: Gallium is used in chips, LEDs and radar. Almost all primary gallium is produced in China, which began restricting its export in 2023.

options.label: Tungsten
options.text: Tungsten makes cutting tools and armour-piercing ammunition. China mines about 79%.

options.label: Platinum
options.text: South Africa mines about 71% of the world's platinum, used in catalytic converters and hydrogen electrolysers.

options.label: Iron ore
options.text: Iron ore is the bulk trade behind steel. Australia (38%) and Brazil (16%) ship most of it, largely to China.

scenes.title: The world redrawn by mining
scenes.text: Here each country is resized by how much it mines. Watch Congo swell for cobalt, Indonesia for nickel and China for rare earths, while most of the map shrinks to almost nothing.

scenes.title: What is still in the ground
scenes.text: Production is not the same as reserves. China mines 69% of rare earths but holds about half of known reserves; Brazil has a quarter and barely mines them yet. Chile holds the largest lithium reserves. The towers show known reserves.

scenes.title: Everything flows to China
scenes.text: Ores and concentrates travel to where they are refined, and that is overwhelmingly China. In 2024 Chile and Peru shipped it over $36 billion of copper ore; Australia and Zimbabwe sent lithium ore, Congo cobalt, Myanmar rare earths.

scenes.title: Bread for Egypt
scenes.text: Food is concentrated too. Egypt is one of the world's largest wheat importers, and most of it comes across the Black Sea. Russia's wheat sales to Egypt nearly doubled in value from 2021 to 2024, to about $3 billion; Ukraine kept supplying despite the war. Play the years.

captions.2022: Russia invades Ukraine; Black Sea ports close until a UN-brokered grain deal in July.
captions.2023: Russia leaves the grain deal in July; Ukraine ships through its own corridor.

scenes.title: Breakfast from a few places
scenes.text: Pick a crop. Two West African neighbours, Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, grow almost half the world's cocoa. Brazil grows nearly a third of its coffee and over a third of its soybeans. Indonesia and Malaysia make four-fifths of all palm oil.
